newsitem.title: USA: Hundreds of homes flooded, many evacuated in U.S..
newsitem.headline: Hundreds of homes flooded, many evacuated in U.S..

text.p: California floods kept tens of thousands of people out of their homes on Saturday, but elsewhere in the storm-hit western United States receding rivers let flood victims return home to start cleaning up.

An estimated 80,000 people evacuated from four towns north of Sacramento, the California state capital, spent a second night in shelters or other temporary housing after the surging Feather River broke through a levee, flooding about 450 homes and 20 square miles (52 sq km) of farmland, officials said.

Only the roofs of dozens of homes were visible amid the murky brown water that stretched as far as the eye could see. Families and pets stranded on the roofs of houses were pulled to safety in daring helicopter rescues.

Dick Hayes, a spokesman for the Yuba County Office of Emergency Services, said there was no chance of evacuees being allowed back into their homes on Saturday. "Not at all. We're not even close," he said.

A plan to channel some of the floodwater back into the Feather River further south failed and the water spread toward the towns of Olivehurst and West Linda, he said. Sandbagging of Olivehurst homes was under way and officials planned to dump boulders into the levee break to try to stem the flow.

The flooding, 50 miles (80 km) north of Sacramento, was some of the most serious caused by a week of torrential storms across the western United States that have killed 18 people and caused hundreds of millions of dollars in damage. Washington state, Oregon, Idaho and Nevada have also been hit by floods, mudslides, road closures and power outages.
California Gov. Pete Wilson asked President Bill Clinton for federal disaster aid on Friday after declaring states of emergency in 37 of California's 58 counties because of floods.

Officials said the California flooding was some of the worst in the state's history. Wilson on Saturday sent California Agriculture Secretary Ann Veneman to tour flood-damaged areas in the state's flood-hit central valley, a leading farming area.
Clinton on Friday made federal disaster relief aid available to several storm-ravaged areas of Nevada.
Skies were overcast in northern California on Saturday but residents had a welcome break from rain.
In Reno, Nevada, cleanup was under way after the Truckee River burst its banks earlier this week, pouring muddy water through the downtown area and forcing some casinos to close.
Residents of the Guerneville area in the northern California wine country were also returning home to begin the unpleasant task of cleaning out mud and debris.
Flooding persisted in other areas because reservoirs, overflowing after warm temperatures melted Sierra Nevada snow, were forced to release water into already high rivers.

One troublespot was around Modesto, in California's central valley 80 miles (130 km) southeast of San Francisco, were the Tuolumne River was at a record 14 feet (4.2 metres) above flood stage, causing the worst flooding since the 1950s, city spokeswoman Renee Ledbetter said.
Some 800 homes in the Modesto area have been evacuated and between 2,000 and 3,000 people moved out, she said. An unknown number of homes flooded, she added.

Several levees broke along the Tuolumne and San Joaquin rivers early on Saturday, flooding agricultural areas. There was a "high possibility" this would force evacuations in the nearby town of Grayson, she said. Officials hoped to see water levels on the Tuolumne River drop by Saturday evening.

Cooler, drier weather brought relief to Washington and Oregon, pounded by more than a week of snow and heavy rain. "Things are getting better," said Ken Keim of the Oregon Emergency Management Division. "The water is going down slowly."
About 21,000 people in the Ashland, Oregon, area remained dependent on drinking water brought in by National Guard troops after a treatment plant was damaged by flooding.

In the Seattle area, two major bridges were closed indefinitely due to damage from mudslides, cutting off neighborhoods. Dozens of people were kept out of homes perched precariously on shifting earth.
